evidence: Caes. B.G. 1.13.6: magis virtūte … quam dolō
terms.comment: Any trick or ruse; the plural dolī are the schemes of comedy’s slaves. In law, dolus malus is fraud. “Play fair” is “without tricks”: sine dolō.

terms.gloss: a trick, a deception, an intrigue
evidence: Ter. And. 212: faciam in nūptiīs fallāciam
Cic. Att. 1.1.1: sine fūcō ac fallāciīs (Lewis & Short)

terms.comment: From Greek τέχνη; “ante-classical” in Lewis & Short, that is, the comedians’ word.

terms.gloss: a catch, a trick (in words or in a deal)

evidence: Ter. And. 1.3.6: cui verba dare difficile est (Lewis & Short s.v. verbum)
Plaut. Merc. 3.4.19: pulchrē ōs sublēvit patrī (Lewis & Short s.v. sublinō)
terms.comment: Literally “to smear someone’s face”, from the prank played on a sleeper (Lewis & Short).

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: ante-classical and late; Cicero uses it twice, only in proverbial phrases. Classical prose says fraudāre.

phrases.latin: dolus an virtūs, quis in hoste requīrat?
phrases.english: trickery or courage: who would ask which, against an enemy?

phrases.latin: nam dolī nōn dolī sunt, nisi astū colās
phrases.english: for tricks aren’t tricks unless you work them cleverly

phrases.latin: Lūditō lēgitimē, absque technīs ac dolō malō.
phrases.english: Play fair, without tricks or cheating.

phrases.latin: Tibi ōs est sublitum plānē et probē.
phrases.english: You’ve been duped good and proper.
